entries.overview: The thick-walled lower left pumping chamber of the heart, forming the pointed tip (apex) of the heart.
entries.function: Receives oxygen-rich blood from the left atrium and pumps it through the aortic valve to the entire body.

facts: Has the thickest muscular wall of any heart chamber because it pushes blood against high systemic pressure.
Separates from the left atrium via the mitral valve and exits through the aortic valve.
Shares a thick muscular divider called the interventricular septum with the right ventricle.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Internal Structure of the Heart
Wikipedia — Ventricle (heart)

entries.overview: The triangular lower right heart chamber sitting behind the breastbone on the front of the heart.
entries.function: Pumps oxygen-poor blood upward through the pulmonary valve into the lungs to pick up fresh oxygen.

facts: Generates roughly one-sixth the pressure of the left ventricle because the lung vessels offer low resistance.
Receives blood from the right atrium across the tricuspid valve.
Tapers upward into a smooth outflow cone leading to the pulmonary trunk.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Internal Structure of the Heart
Wikipedia — Ventricle (heart)

entries.overview: The upper back chamber of the heart perched behind the pulmonary trunk and facing the esophagus.
entries.function: Collects freshly oxygenated blood returning from both lungs via four pulmonary veins and fills the left ventricle.

facts: Forms most of the posterior base of the heart.
Contains mostly smooth interior walls except inside its small ear-like appendage (left auricle).
Contracts at the end of ventricular filling to top off left ventricular volume before each beat.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Internal Structure of the Heart
Wikipedia — Atrium (heart)

entries.overview: The upper right receiving chamber forming the right outer border of the heart.
entries.function: Gathers oxygen-poor venous blood from the upper and lower body as well as from the heart wall itself.

facts: Receives blood from the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, and coronary sinus.
Houses the sinoatrial node, the natural pacemaker that initiates every heartbeat.
Delivers blood downward into the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Internal Structure of the Heart
Wikipedia — Atrium (heart)

entries.overview: The curved upper loop of the body’s largest artery arching backward over the left main airway.
entries.function: Routes oxygenated blood from the ascending aorta downward toward the chest while feeding three major head and arm trunks.

facts: Branches in order into the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, and left subclavian artery.
Contains stretch sensors (baroreceptors) that help regulate blood pressure.
Continues behind the left lung root as the descending thoracic aorta.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — The Aorta and Its Major Branches
Wikipedia — Aortic arch

entries.overview: The chest segment of the descending aorta running along the left side of the spine down to the diaphragm.
entries.function: Supplies oxygenated blood to the chest wall, intercostal spaces, bronchial airways, and esophagus.

facts: Gives off paired posterior intercostal arteries that travel between the ribs.
Passes through the aortic opening of the diaphragm at vertebral level T12 to become the abdominal aorta.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — The Aorta and Its Major Branches
Wikipedia — Thoracic aorta

entries.overview: The largest artery in the abdomen, descending along the front of the lower spine behind the digestive organs.
entries.function: Distributes oxygenated blood to the stomach, liver, intestines, kidneys, and lower trunk before splitting into the pelvis.

facts: Gives off three unpaired digestive trunks: the celiac trunk, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric arteries.
Sends paired renal arteries directly outward to each kidney.
Splits near lumbar vertebra L4 into the left and right common iliac arteries.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — The Aorta and Its Major Branches
Wikipedia — Abdominal aorta

entries.overview: A short, wide arterial vessel arching upward from the top of the right ventricle inside the chest.
entries.function: Carries oxygen-poor blood out of the heart and splits into the left and right pulmonary arteries to the lungs.

facts: Unique among systemic trunks because it carries deoxygenated blood.
Divides beneath the aortic arch into left and right pulmonary arteries entering each lung.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Pulmonary Circulation
Wikipedia — Pulmonary artery

entries.overview: A short, wide vertical vein entering the top back of the right atrium inside the upper chest.
entries.function: Returns oxygen-poor venous blood from the head, neck, arms, and upper chest wall back to the heart.

facts: Forms where the left and right brachiocephalic veins merge behind the first rib.
Has no internal venous valves, relying on gravity and breathing pressure to assist blood flow.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Systemic Veins
Wikipedia — Superior vena cava

entries.overview: The large central vein rising along the right side of the lumbar spine inside the back of the abdomen.
entries.function: Drains venous blood from the legs, pelvis, kidneys, liver, and abdominal wall upward toward the heart.

facts: Forms near the fifth lumbar vertebra from the merger of both common iliac veins.
Receives renal veins directly and passes behind the liver before piercing the diaphragm.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Systemic Veins
Wikipedia — Inferior vena cava

entries.overview: A major branch of the left coronary artery running down the front groove between the heart’s two ventricles.
entries.function: Delivers roughly half of the oxygenated blood feeding the thick pumping wall of the left ventricle.

facts: Often called the left anterior descending (LAD) artery in clinical medicine.
Feeds the front wall of both ventricles and the front two-thirds of the interventricular septum.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Coronary Circulation
Wikipedia — Left anterior descending artery

entries.overview: A main heart-wall artery branching from the base of the aorta and coursing along the right border of the heart.
entries.function: Supplies oxygenated blood to the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, and the heart’s pacemaker tissue.

facts: Travels in the groove between the right atrium and right ventricle toward the back of the heart.
In most people, feeds both the sinoatrial node and atrioventricular node.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Coronary Circulation
Wikipedia — Right coronary artery

entries.overview: A major ascending neck artery rising directly from the aortic arch beside the windpipe.
entries.function: Delivers high-pressure oxygenated blood up the left side of the neck to feed the brain, face, and scalp.

facts: Travels inside the protective carotid sheath alongside the internal jugular vein.
Splits near the upper edge of the larynx into the internal and external carotid arteries.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — The Aorta and Its Major Branches
Wikipedia — Common carotid artery

entries.overview: A deep, wide neck vein descending vertically from the base of the skull inside the carotid sheath.
entries.function: Drains venous blood from the brain’s dural sinuses along with the face and deep neck back toward the chest.

facts: Begins at the jugular foramen of the skull and joins the subclavian vein behind the collarbone.
Visible pressure pulsations in the lower neck reflect pressure inside the right atrium.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Systemic Veins
Wikipedia — Internal jugular vein

entries.overview: A large, midline blood-filled channel tucked within the tough upper fold of dura mater along the skull roof.
entries.function: Collects used venous blood and absorbed cerebrospinal fluid from the top of both cerebral hemispheres.

facts: Unlike ordinary veins, dural sinuses have rigid fibrous walls with no muscle or valves.
Empties at the back of the skull into the transverse sinuses leading to the internal jugular veins.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Systemic Veins
Wikipedia — Superior sagittal sinus

entries.overview: The main arterial trunk descending along the inner front side of the upper arm.
entries.function: Supplies oxygenated blood to upper arm muscles before dividing below the elbow to feed the forearm and hand.

facts: Continues directly from the axillary artery and splits at the elbow crease into the radial and ulnar arteries.
Its pulse is easily felt just medial to the biceps tendon and is the standard site for cuff blood-pressure measurement.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Upper Limb Arteries
Wikipedia — Brachial artery

entries.overview: The thumb-side forearm artery running close to the skin near the outer edge of the wrist.
entries.function: Brings oxygenated blood along the thumb side of the forearm into the deep palmar arch supplying the hand.

facts: Lies directly over the flat front surface of the radius bone at the wrist, making it the classic spot to check a radial pulse.
Loops across the base of the thumb to meet branches from the ulnar artery inside the palm.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Upper Limb Arteries
Wikipedia — Radial artery

entries.overview: A paired pelvic artery formed where the abdominal aorta forks just above the brim of the pelvis.
entries.function: Channels oxygenated blood outward and downward to supply both the pelvic organs and the lower limbs.

facts: Each common iliac artery divides near the sacroiliac joint into an internal and an external iliac artery.
The internal branch feeds the pelvis and gluteal muscles while the external branch continues into the thigh.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Lower Limb Arteries
Wikipedia — Common iliac artery

entries.overview: The major artery entering the front upper thigh right below the crease of the groin.
entries.function: Supplies the powerful muscles and tissues of the thigh and continues behind the knee to feed the leg and foot.

facts: Passes superficially through the femoral triangle in the groin before diving deep along the inner thigh.
Gives off the deep femoral artery to nourish the thigh before becoming the popliteal artery behind the knee.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Lower Limb Arteries
Wikipedia — Femoral artery

entries.overview: The longest vein in the human body, running just beneath the skin from the inner foot all the way to the groin.
entries.function: Returns venous blood from the superficial tissues of the foot, lower leg, and inner thigh to the femoral vein.

facts: Begins in front of the inner ankle bone and ascends along the medial leg and thigh.
Contains one-way valves and is frequently harvested for coronary or peripheral arterial bypass grafts.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e — Systemic Veins
Wikipedia — Great saphenous vein
